title: [Spiritual Traditions] The Bhagavad Gita on Action, Duty and Attachment
summary: Begin with Arjuna's moral conflict and follow the Gita's account of duty, the enduring self, action without attachment, meditation, devotion and the three qualities of nature. Original community-performance examples distinguish responsible action from dependence on praise or indifference to consequences. Five recall questions with pauses and answers, plus a small reflective application. Source consulted: Bhagavad Gita, Edwin Arnold's public-domain poetic translation The Song Celestial, selected chapters I, II, III, V, VI, IX, XII, XIV and XVIII, https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/2388/pg2388-images.html . Edition and translator information: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2388. This is a focused reading through one historical English translation, not coverage of the whole work or every Hindu interpretation. Metaphysical and devotional teachings are presented as teachings; modern cases and arithmetic are original illustrations.
instructions: Two substantive teachers, ash and sage. Begin directly with Arjuna's conflict. Natural pace; no introductory learning lecture or motivational padding. Explain theological concepts in their setting, distinguish modern applications, and preserve all five seven-second recall pauses with the subsequent answers. No ritual, medical claim or assumed listener belief.

turns.t: Arjuna has arrived at a battle he knows how to fight. He has weapons, training, allies and a charioteer. Then he asks to look closely at the people on the other side. Among the opponents are relatives and respected teachers. His skill has not disappeared, but his reason for using it has collapsed. Winning would mean helping to destroy people whose presence made the prize worth having. He lowers his bow. The Bhagavad Gita begins with that collision between a public responsibility and an intimate moral cost.

turns.t: That makes his problem more difficult than a lack of motivation. You could encourage a nervous competitor by reminding them of the prize. Arjuna has already considered the prize, and it no longer answers his objection. What would a kingdom mean if gaining it required killing the people he loved? He also fears damage to families and their obligations across generations. His distress has a physical expression, but it contains an argument. Understanding the Gita requires hearing that argument before hearing Krishna's response to it.

turns.t: Krishna is driving the chariot, but he becomes the teacher in the conversation. He is also presented as divine, which becomes increasingly central to what he teaches. The dialogue belongs within the Mahabharata, the much larger epic. We are going to follow a connected question through selected chapters: how can a person act without being ruled by attachment to what the action might bring? The text answers through duty, knowledge of the self, disciplined action and devotion. It does not offer a single trick for feeling less stressed before doing something difficult.

turns.t: Our English source is Edwin Arnold's poetic translation, The Song Celestial. Its language sometimes sounds like Victorian religious poetry because that is what the English rendering is. We will explain the ideas in ordinary speech and identify our own examples as examples. This matters especially with words such as soul, duty and renunciation. Each carries associations in English that may not exactly reproduce the Sanskrit concepts. We are examining a set of teachings in the Gita, rather than treating one translation as the final voice of every Hindu tradition.

turns.t: Look first at the structure of Arjuna's uncertainty. He occupies several relationships at once. As a warrior, he is expected to fight. As a relative, he cares about the people who may die. As a pupil, he reveres teachers facing him. Each relationship seems to make a claim on him. A choice that satisfies one claim violates another. That is why telling him simply to follow his feelings is inadequate. His feelings are responding to real and competing commitments. The crisis concerns which commitment should govern when they cannot all be satisfied.

turns.t: Krishna's initial response is deliberately forceful. He challenges Arjuna's retreat, then offers several kinds of reason for acting. Some concern the enduring self. Some concern a warrior's duty and reputation. Others concern the discipline of performing action without seeking its rewards as the basis of one's identity. Those are different arguments, even when they converge on the same instruction in the story. We should not merge them into a vague statement that everything happens for a reason. The dialogue becomes clearer when we can say what each argument is actually doing.

turns.t: Take dharma, a central term often rendered as duty in this discussion. Here duty is situated. It concerns a particular person, in a particular role, within an ordered moral and social world. It is not merely whatever activity feels personally exciting. Krishna treats Arjuna's warrior role as carrying obligations that discomfort does not automatically cancel. That explains why the question is not simply whether Arjuna enjoys fighting. It is whether refusing this action would itself abandon something he is responsible for upholding. His refusal must be assessed as a choice too.

turns.t: A modern analogy can show the structure without equating ordinary life with a battlefield. Imagine a music organiser who has promised to arrange sound for a small community performance. A close friend wants the event cancelled after an argument with another performer. Friendship pulls one way; commitments to everyone else pull another. The organiser cannot settle the matter by declaring the strongest feeling sacred. They need to ask what was promised, who depends on it and whether the request is justified. That is our invented example, not an incident from the Gita.

turns.t: The analogy has a boundary. The Gita's account of social duty includes a traditional division of social roles, discussed explicitly near the end. We should not quietly translate that entire order into the modern idea of choosing a career that expresses your individuality. Those are different frameworks. Nor does a boss acquire Krishna's authority by saying a task is your duty. When we apply an idea today, we still have to examine whether the claimed obligation is legitimate. A role can carry a real responsibility without making every demand from its holder right.

turns.t: There is also an important difference between difficulty and wrongdoing. A task may be unpleasant because it requires patience, sacrifice or admitting a mistake. A different task may be unpleasant because it requires deceiving someone. Those cannot be treated as the same obstacle to overcome. In the performance example, telling your friend you will keep an existing commitment might be difficult but defensible. Lying to the performers about their payment would raise a different problem. Calling both situations a test of discipline would erase the very moral judgment the situation requires.

turns.t: The battlefield does not disappear once these ideas become useful in ordinary life. Within the story, Krishna really does urge Arjuna to fight. A reading that turns every opponent into a private bad habit may offer a metaphor, but it changes the level of the narrative. The text confronts action under conditions where harm and obligation are entangled. That is one reason the opening is so powerful. Arjuna cannot solve the problem simply by becoming more efficient. He needs a changed understanding of the action, the actor and what is at stake.

turns.t: He also becomes a questioning student rather than an unthinking instrument. In successive chapters he asks why action is required if knowledge is so important, why renunciation is praised alongside work, and how a restless mind could possibly become steady. His questions expose tensions that an attentive reader might notice. The teaching proceeds through those tensions. So the relationship is not just an authority delivering a slogan and demanding compliance. The poem makes space for Arjuna to state why an answer has not yet resolved his difficulty, and then develops another part of the explanation.

turns.t: The first major shift concerns what the self is. In chapter two, Krishna distinguishes the perishing body from an enduring self. Bodies pass through childhood, youth and age, and the teaching extends that pattern to taking on another body. Arnold renders this through the image of changing worn clothing. The self is presented as something that weapons cannot cut and fire cannot burn. This is a metaphysical claim within the text. It changes the meaning of death in Krishna's argument; it is not a laboratory finding about what happens after death.

turns.t: Notice what that claim is meant to loosen. Arjuna's vision is dominated by the immediate destruction of bodies and relationships. Krishna places that scene within a larger account of existence, where embodied life is not the whole of the self. If you accept the account, loss is interpreted differently. If you do not accept it, you can still understand how the argument works without pretending its premise has been demonstrated to you. The lesson is intellectually clearer when the premise remains visible than when it is disguised as a modern discovery about energy.

turns.t: The word energy would be particularly misleading here. Physical conservation laws concern quantities defined and measured within physical models. They do not by themselves establish a person's continuing consciousness after death. The Gita's enduring self belongs to a different kind of account. You do not improve either physics or the Gita by using one as an unexamined proof of the other. In this passage, the relevant idea is that the deepest identity is not exhausted by a changing body. That is the teaching to understand before accepting, rejecting or comparing it.

turns.t: The clothing image can nevertheless clarify the distinction the text is drawing. A garment changes while its wearer is treated as persisting. The analogy makes continuity through bodily change imaginable. It does not independently prove that the wearer exists beyond the body, because that is precisely the premise under discussion. This is a useful way to read a strong image: ask which relationship it illuminates. Here it illuminates replacement and continuity. It cannot settle every question about memory, personality or the conditions under which a particular individual remains the same person.

turns.t: Nor should the enduring self be turned into an excuse to disregard suffering. Even inside this dialogue, the teaching develops standards for action, self-restraint, compassion and responsibility. A listener cannot reasonably extract the line about the self being unharmed and infer that anything done to bodies is therefore acceptable. That would skip the argument about which action is rightful. The narrative gives Krishna a specific teaching role and Arjuna a specific crisis. It does not hand every person a universal permission to cause harm while declaring their own mind detached.

turns.t: There are now two levels on the table. One concerns the situation: what responsibility does Arjuna have? The other concerns identity: what is the being that acts and undergoes change? Krishna brings the levels together, but they should remain distinguishable. Someone may accept an obligation while rejecting the account of rebirth. Another person may believe in an enduring self while disagreeing about a particular duty. Keeping the levels separate helps us see the text's actual architecture. It also prevents us from assuming that one compelling idea has automatically established all the others.

turns.t: First recall question. Why is Arjuna's opening problem more than ordinary procrastination, and what does Krishna's distinction between body and enduring self add to the discussion? Give yourself a moment to name the conflict and the additional premise. You do not need Sanskrit terminology. Focus on what Arjuna is afraid an apparently successful action will cost, then on the change of perspective Krishna introduces. A useful answer should explain why a simple promise of victory would not resolve the original objection.

turns.t: Arjuna faces competing obligations to his role, relatives and teachers. Victory itself could destroy people and relationships he values, so increasing his motivation does not answer his moral concern. Krishna then introduces the teaching that the body perishes while the self endures. That places death within a larger metaphysical picture. It is one part of Krishna's answer, alongside duty and disciplined action, rather than a proven scientific fact or a permission to ignore harm. With those distinctions in place, we can examine the Gita's most frequently borrowed teaching: acting without attachment to the fruits.

turns.t: A fruit is what an action produces or promises to produce. In the Gita's discussion, fruits include rewards that can make action a source of bondage. You act for a desired result, cling to it and become governed by its arrival or absence. Krishna instructs Arjuna to act while relinquishing that attachment. Both halves matter. If we remember only relinquishment, we may hear an invitation to do nothing. If we remember only action, we may preserve the same restless pursuit of reward that the teaching is trying to transform.

turns.t: Imagine our organiser preparing the sound for the performance. There is a legitimate result to aim at: the audience should hear the musicians clearly. Planning toward that result is part of doing the task well. But suppose the organiser's private condition is that everyone must praise them afterwards or the evening counts as humiliation. Now a useful aim has become a demand that the world deliver personal vindication. That demand can reshape their behaviour before the event, during a mistake and after the applause. It is a different relationship to the result.

turns.t: Before the event, they might spend their limited rehearsal time imagining praise instead of checking the equipment. During it, they might conceal a fault because admitting it threatens their image. Afterwards, they might ignore the musicians' needs while searching for compliments. The outward activity still looks like organising a show, but attention is being pulled toward self-confirmation. Our example illustrates attachment through a particular pattern of conduct. The Gita's religious purpose goes further, toward liberation from the binding character of action, but this pattern makes the practical distinction easier to see.

turns.t: Relinquishing the demand for praise does not mean unplugging the speakers and claiming that outcomes do not matter. The organiser still chooses equipment, checks the room and responds when the audience cannot hear. The change lies in what governs the work. Doing it responsibly becomes less dependent on receiving a personally flattering result. They can want the music to be heard and still recognise that applause is not entirely theirs to command. A delayed train, an ill performer or a change of audience mood may affect the evening despite careful preparation.

turns.t: The Gita joins this discipline to equanimity, steadiness through success and failure. Equanimity is easy to mistake for feeling nothing. In this argument it concerns the actor's relation to changing circumstances. If every favourable result makes you grandiose and every unfavourable result makes you abandon your responsibilities, circumstances have acquired enormous control over your conduct. A steadier actor can respond to what happened without having to rebuild their identity around it. The text gives that steadiness a spiritual foundation; our event example shows one practical difference it would make.

turns.t: Suppose the first song sounds poor because a microphone was positioned badly. There are at least three responses. One is panic and self-condemnation. Another is indifference disguised as detachment. A third is to adjust the microphone, acknowledge the problem and continue attending to the performance. The third response includes concern for consequences. It simply does not require a theatrical judgment about whether the organiser is a brilliant person or a worthless one. Correcting an action and defending an identity are different tasks, and attachment can make the second consume the first.

turns.t: That distinction also explains why planning is compatible with this form of nonattachment. Planning estimates which actions may bring about worthwhile results. Attachment makes a particular result the condition of inner security or the sole reason to act. You can revise a plan when conditions change without worshipping the plan's original promise. The organiser might discover that the hall has fewer working sockets than expected. Responsible action means changing the setup. Insisting that reality obey the imagined perfect evening would be the opposite of skill, however confidently that insistence was expressed.

turns.t: Here is a small invented budget of attention. The organiser has sixty minutes before the rehearsal. Twenty minutes go to checking connections, twenty-five to testing the sound with performers and fifteen to fixing what the test reveals. Those periods total sixty minutes. This is not a sacred timetable or a prescription from the text. It makes a concrete point: work directed toward a result contains testing and correction. If all sixty minutes are spent rehearsing the compliments one hopes to receive, the external responsibility has been displaced by attachment to an imagined reward.

turns.t: Chapter three makes the action side of the teaching explicit. Arjuna asks why he should undertake this terrible action if another form of understanding is superior. Krishna replies that simply avoiding outward work does not establish freedom. Living beings act; even maintaining embodied life requires activity. A person who restrains their outward behaviour while mentally dwelling on desired objects has not necessarily renounced attachment. The visible stillness can conceal inward preoccupation. So the distinction between an active person and an inactive person cannot by itself tell us who is spiritually free.

turns.t: The organiser could resign from the show, then spend the entire evening checking whether the replacement receives more praise. Outward withdrawal has left the competition intact. Conversely, they could remain involved, handle a dull technical task and give credit fairly without making recognition the point. That comparison is useful because it separates the location of the body from the orientation of the mind. The Gita does not reduce spiritual discipline to being busy, either. It asks how activity is performed and toward what understanding or devotion it is directed.

turns.t: Krishna also introduces a wider social reason for action. In chapter three, the conduct of exemplary people influences others, and his own activity is presented as sustaining order even though he has no personal prize left to obtain. Action can serve the maintenance of the world rather than private acquisition. This takes the teaching beyond a solitary person's mood. Your conduct enters a network of dependences and examples. The question becomes whether your way of acting supports the world you share, including people who are not present to reward you.

turns.t: In the performance case, the organiser's checking routine affects more than sound quality. A younger volunteer watches how mistakes are handled. If the organiser blames a performer to protect their reputation, that becomes a model of leadership. If they state the problem plainly and repair it, a different model is transmitted. The effect is not magical and the volunteer may still choose otherwise. But the case helps us understand why Krishna discusses exemplary action. A person's visible conduct can teach a standard even when no formal instruction is being given.

turns.t: The chapter also uses sacrifice to place action within a reciprocal order. In the text's religious account, human activity, offerings, divine powers, rain and food form an interconnected cycle. Eating while giving nothing back is condemned. We should hear the religious account as it stands before translating it into an ecological slogan. The central practical contrast is between taking benefits as if one were entirely self-sufficient and acknowledging an order of support. The actor does not create all the conditions of their life alone, however prominent their own effort feels.

turns.t: Our organiser depends on people who built the hall, maintain the electrical system, teach musicians and make instruments. Acknowledging those dependencies could change how they use the venue and treat its staff. That is a modern extension of the theme of reciprocity, not a claim that maintaining cables is the original meaning of Vedic sacrifice. The distinction allows an analogy to be useful without swallowing the source. It also challenges the fantasy that a successful performance belongs entirely to the one person standing nearest the applause at the end.

turns.t: Chapter five returns to the apparent conflict between renunciation and work. Krishna presents both as capable of leading toward the highest good, while favouring disciplined action in this exchange. The renouncer is described through freedom from craving and aversion, not simply departure from ordinary activity. Arnold gives the image of a lotus leaf remaining unstained by water. The action occurs, but it need not adhere to the actor as possessive attachment. The image helps explain why working and renouncing are not treated as simple opposites in the dialogue.

turns.t: Craving and aversion can pull in opposite directions while creating a similar loss of freedom. Craving says that a desirable experience must be obtained. Aversion says that an undesirable experience must be escaped at any cost. The organiser might crave admiration and hate the discomfort of receiving criticism. Both can make an honest sound check difficult. Freedom from those pulls would permit a more accurate hearing of the problem. In the Gita, the discipline belongs to spiritual release; in our case, we can see how it changes the quality of an ordinary response.

turns.t: There is a further complication near the close of the text. Renunciation is itself distinguished according to motive. Leaving a responsibility from confusion is not the same as relinquishing attachment while carrying it out. Avoiding work merely because it is uncomfortable is not praised as the highest form of renunciation. This prevents a convenient loophole: calling every abandoned obligation spiritual freedom. The relevant questions include whether the action was rightly required, why it was abandoned and what attachment remained. An impressive label cannot decide those questions on its own.

turns.t: Equally, changing or ending an unjust arrangement is not automatically the avoidance being criticised. Our modern application has to establish the obligation before it can discuss carrying it out. If the organiser discovers that a promised arrangement depends on deceiving the musicians, correcting the arrangement may be the responsible action. The text's lesson about steadfastness does not remove the need to distinguish right action from wrong action. In fact, chapter eighteen explicitly distinguishes actions performed without regard to injury or consequence from the disciplined action being commended. That distinction will matter again when we discuss the qualities.

turns.t: Second recall question. The organiser wants the audience to hear the music clearly, but also wants universal praise. Which desire belongs to the task's practical aim, and how might attachment to praise interfere with it? Then explain why giving up all preparation would not count as the kind of renunciation Krishna recommends here. Try to answer with a specific behaviour, such as concealing a microphone fault or refusing useful criticism, rather than only saying that attachment is bad.

turns.t: Clear sound is the practical aim that guides preparation and correction. Attachment to universal praise makes personal validation govern the work, perhaps leading the organiser to hide a fault or reject feedback. Abandoning preparation would neglect the responsibility; it would not necessarily remove that attachment. Krishna's teaching joins action with relinquishment of possessive dependence on its fruits. The organiser can test the system, correct mistakes and care about the musicians while letting go of the demand that the evening establish their worth. The action remains serious, even when the reward is no longer sovereign.

turns.t: Action without attachment requires a mind capable of staying with something other than its latest impulse. Chapter six develops the discipline of meditation. The setting is quiet, the posture steady and attention directed inward and toward Krishna. The text describes a mind like a lamp protected from wind. That image supplies a contrast with ordinary agitation. A flame exposed to every gust cannot hold a steady shape. Likewise, a mind pulled immediately into each desire and disturbance has difficulty remaining with the understanding it is trying to cultivate.

turns.t: Arjuna's objection is refreshingly concrete. The mind feels restless and difficult to restrain, as though one were trying to control the wind. Krishna does not answer that restlessness proves Arjuna is uniquely defective. He acknowledges the difficulty and presents practice and restraint as the way forward. The chapter also says that when the mind wanders, it should be brought back. Wandering is therefore anticipated within the instruction. The work is in returning, rather than inventing a fantasy that a sincere beginner will never encounter distraction again.

turns.t: Consider the difference between two versions of returning. In one, the organiser sits quietly, remembers tomorrow's performance and immediately starts designing an imaginary victory speech. On noticing that, they angrily decide the entire attempt has failed. In the other, they recognise where attention went and return to the chosen focus. The second version performs the actual corrective movement. The first adds another drama about the self. This is an illustrative comparison, not a clinical promise. In the chapter, the discipline serves a spiritual aim that includes union, knowledge and devotion.

turns.t: A particularly useful detail is moderation. Krishna does not praise unlimited fasting, unlimited eating, excessive sleep or exhausting wakefulness as the route to this discipline. The chapter relates steadiness to a measured pattern of activity and rest. That complicates the idea that spirituality must be demonstrated through punishing intensity. A person who is continually making their ordinary conditions more chaotic may be working against the steadiness they seek. The text connects the inward practice with a way of living, rather than presenting a few isolated minutes as entirely separate from everything around them.

turns.t: The movement from attention to conduct appears again in how the accomplished practitioner sees others. The chapter describes a relation to living beings that reaches beyond partiality to friends and hostility to enemies. It asks the practitioner to recognise others through a shared or universal life and through comparison with oneself. This is not simply concentration for better personal performance. Concentration is placed inside a transformed orientation toward existence. If the resulting person becomes exceptionally focused but increasingly contemptuous of everyone else, an essential part of the chapter has been left behind.

turns.t: In our performance example, attention could make the organiser very good at detecting mistakes while still cruel to the performers. Technical concentration alone would not answer the Gita's broader demand. The question is how attention, self-understanding and conduct fit together. Can the organiser hear a problem without treating the person who made it as an enemy? Can they remain useful when the mistake belongs to someone they dislike? Those questions bring the inner discipline back into a social setting. The goal is not a private calm purchased by refusing to notice other people.

turns.t: The dialogue also considers incomplete practice. Arjuna asks what happens to someone who begins with faith but fails to reach the goal. Krishna's answer includes rebirth and the continuation of spiritual progress across lives. That is part of the religious picture, rather than an account of how a single training session affects the brain. Its narrative function is to challenge despair about sincere but unfinished effort. The aspiring practitioner is not portrayed as necessarily erased by failing to attain perfection immediately. The larger horizon changes how incompletion is interpreted.

turns.t: That devotional orientation becomes unmistakable in chapter nine. Krishna describes himself as the source and support of the world, while also exceeding the visible world. He is not merely a wise colleague giving Arjuna helpful suggestions. The relation between the human actor and the divine is part of the answer to attachment. An action can be offered rather than possessed as a private achievement. Food, gifts, worship and other ordinary acts are drawn into that relation. Devotion changes to whom, and for what, the action is understood to belong.

turns.t: One memorable passage says that a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water can be accepted when offered with devotion. The emphasis shifts away from the material grandeur of the gift and toward the manner of offering. Within that religious frame, a small act is not disqualified because it cannot compete with a wealthy person's display. The comparison also exposes a possible form of attachment: making an offering mainly to establish one's own importance. A modest gift sincerely directed toward the divine and an impressive gift directed toward self-display are not spiritually identical.

turns.t: Chapter twelve begins with another question from Arjuna. He asks about those devoted to Krishna in manifest form and those oriented toward the unmanifest. The chapter does not simply declare that all objects of attention are interchangeable. It speaks about approaches to the ultimate within its own theological framework.

turns.t: Chapter eighteen brings together renunciation, knowledge, action and devotion without making them a simple menu of unrelated techniques. It also tells Arjuna to reflect and then act, before renewing the appeal to seek refuge in Krishna. The closing movement includes both consideration and trust. Arjuna's response is that his confusion has lifted and that he will act. The story has moved from paralysis in the chariot to a settled commitment. turns.t: We can now recognise three connected dimensions. Knowledge changes the understanding of the self and action. Disciplined work changes the actor's relation to reward. turns.t: Chapter fourteen names three qualities, or gunas: sattva, rajas and tamas. Arnold renders them through words such as goodness or soothfastness, passion and ignorance. For an initial grasp, think of clarity, restless striving and obscuring inertia. Those plain descriptions are approximations. The text presents the qualities as features of nature that bind the embodied self in different ways. It is a philosophical and religious model, not a modern personality test. The point is to understand its distinctions and how they are applied to knowledge, action and the actor.

turns.t: Sattva is associated with illumination and relative clarity. Rajas involves appetite, agitation and attachment to activity and its results. Tamas involves obscurity, heedlessness and inertia. A tempting simplification would make them three permanent kinds of person, with you choosing the flattering category for yourself. But the chapter describes qualities becoming predominant and competing with one another. That makes the model more dynamic. It can distinguish tendencies within experience and conduct, rather than requiring us to label one whole human being permanently clear and another permanently dark.

turns.t: There is an even more surprising detail. Sattva also binds, through attachment to happiness and knowledge. The highest aim is therefore not merely to acquire the most respectable attachment. turns.t: Our organiser supplies three possible patterns without turning the model into a diagnosis. In one pattern, they see the equipment clearly, fulfil the commitment and accept correction. In another, they are consumed by comparison, praise and the need to dominate the evening. In a third, they ignore obvious problems, fail to check what was promised and refuse to consider who may be affected. These are illustrations of different orientations toward action. They are not claims that the Gita has measured the organiser's biology or discovered a fixed type hidden in their body.

turns.t: Chapter eighteen sharpens the difference through its account of action. The action associated with clarity is performed as a responsibility without attachment, hatred or hunger for personal gain. The restless action is driven by desire and the sense of self. The obscured action is undertaken without adequate regard for consequences, injury or capacity. That last description is especially important. It prevents nonattachment from being reduced to recklessness. The text can criticise heedlessness about consequences while also teaching release from attachment to the fruits. Those are different relations to what an action brings about.

turns.t: The qualities are also applied to understanding. The text contrasts a vision of unity, a vision absorbed in separate things and a narrow understanding that clings to a fragment as if it were everything. A fragment is mistaken for the whole, and the person no longer investigates beyond it. The problem is not merely possessing limited information. It is treating that limit as complete understanding and closing off the possibility that the situation contains more.

turns.t: The qualities can initially be understood as clarity, restless striving and obscuring inertia. Even clarity can bind when the person becomes attached to its happiness, knowledge or identity. turns.t: For example, the commitment might be to send a draft for feedback. The responsibility is to send something honest and usable by the agreed time. turns.t: When Arjuna commits to act, the poem presents a changed actor, not merely a refreshed burst of energy. The conversation has joined an account of duty to an account of self, a discipline of action and a relation of devotion. For your own small task, the immediate question is concrete: can you fulfil the legitimate commitment, attend to its consequences and release the demand that the result confirm your importance? Carry out the action, then look honestly at what happened. That gives the teaching something real to meet, beyond an attractive sentence about letting go.
